posts.name: Kevin Maro
posts.text:
I've been seeing a lot of doomsday-level short positions on AI infra over the past few weeks. The basic thesis: if Jensen has been propping up the price of his chips through circular financing and that unravels, we could find out the chips these neoclouds are renting out are actually worth... let's just say half of what they paid for them. If that happens, they'll be devoured by the debt they've taken on. $NBIS, for example, has $14B in debt on its balance sheet as a ~$35B company.

And it doesn't stop at Nvidia. If the market decides an H100 or Blackwell is really worth half, that resets the price for everything priced against it. Google's TPUs are priced to compete with Nvidia's current chips, so they'd get marked down too. Then it moves down the line: GPU rental rates, neocloud contracts, data center valuations, the power deals, the memory and networking suppliers. Every part of the AI stack is anchored to that one number. Pull it down and everything can violently re-rate to the downside.

Btw, this would be VERY bad news for every tech company that's taken on debt. $AMZN, $META, $GOOGL... even they'd get slaughtered (in the short term).

Not financial advice.

posts.text:
A double from here doesn't require a miracle $SNAP 

There is plenty to dislike about Snap. Advertising growth slowing to  just 4%, fewer daily users in North America than a year ago, excessive SBC, regulatory headaches and you got a founder that is obsessed with SPECS, a costly bet on AR hardware with unproven commercial economics

And yet, I increasingly think the stock could work from here

The irony is that Snap may be getting financially interesting just as investors are running out of patience with the company

In Q3, revenue grew 14% yoy, while gross margin expanded by 7pp to 62%. Operating income swung from a loss of $128m to a profit of $77m, and LTM free cash flow increased 88% to $777m

Roughly 93 cents of every incremental revenue dollar flowed through to adjusted EBITDA

That is not a sustainable incremental margin, but it tells you something about the earnings power of this business when management exercises some financial discipline

Advertising is where things could get interesting.
At 4% growth, Snap's advertising business is clearly underperforming. But the underlying performance metrics are overshadowed by the headline number:

(1) App purchase campaign revenue +54% or better, with cost per purchase down ~24%
(2) Web purchase campaign revenue +11%, with purchases up over 31%
(3) Sponsored Snaps revenue +56% sequentially.
(4) Spotlight eCPM +22% yoy, alongside 40% growth in daily viewers
(5) Promoted Places revenue and advertiser adoption both more than doubled sequentially, albeit from a small base

As direct response becomes a larger part of the advertising mix, weakness in brand advertising should become less of a drag on overall growth. If brand advertising stabilizes and improving advertiser returns translate into larger budgets, I see a credible path back to double-digit advertising growth in 2027

Then there is the subscription business. Other revenue grew 84% yoy with more than 30m paying subscribers across Snapchat+, Memories Storage and Lens+. That's equivalent to just over 3% of Snap's 977m MAU

Despite a decline in North American DAUs, revenue grew 13% YoY and ARPU increased 20%, meaning that Snap is getting better at monetising its existing user base

What about Capital allocation? 

Snap spent approximately $601m on share repurchases in the first nine months of 2026. Over the same period, it generated $571m in FCF. Yet shares outstanding, including underlying stock-based awards, increased 3.8% yoy. SBC was approximately $255m in Q3 alone, unforgiveable

posts.name: Gary Black
posts.text:
$NVDA:  This is an absurd take.  When a board pushes out a CEO for having an affair with a subordinate, there is near zero chance the board will suddenly have a change of heart and say they’ve reconsidered, the executive can come back just because the stock has dropped.  The board would look like clowns and lose all credibility with investors.  There is too much practical and legal risk to the firm, even if the relationship was consensual.  

Here is a summary of risks per Grok.
- Sexual harassment and retaliation claims (Title VII and state equivalents): This is the core exposure. A subordinate can later claim the relationship was not truly welcome because of the power differential (the CEO controls compensation, promotions, assignments, and continued employment). Even if it starts consensually, adverse actions after a breakup (denied promotion, poor review, termination, reassignment) support retaliation claims. Other employees can also claim a hostile work environment based on perceived favoritism. In some states (notably California under FEHA), employers face strict liability for supervisor harassment.
- Favoritism and discrimination claims: Co-workers who believe the subordinate receives preferential treatment can sue. Courts have recognized claims where a supervisor’s relationships create a toxic environment of perceived quid pro quo for advancement.
- Policy violations and fiduciary/breach-of-duty issues: Most large companies prohibit or tightly restrict relationships between managers and direct (or indirect) reports, or require disclosure. Non-disclosure or concealment can support claims that the CEO breached duties of loyalty or care to the company. For public companies, boards that fail to address the known risk may face derivative claims from shareholders.
- Reputational, operational, and financial fallout: These situations routinely produce media coverage, internal morale problems, difficulty managing the subordinate’s performance, and board distraction. Settlements are common even in weak cases because of embarrassment. High-profile precedents include the ousters of CEOs at McDonald’s (Steve Easterbrook, later sued for clawback of ~$105 million severance after concealment of other relationships), Intel, Nestlé, Norfolk Southern, and others. Recent reporting has tied similar issues to Nvidia leadership transitions.

Practical Implications 
The firm’s exposure is often larger than pure legal damages (which under Title VII are capped by company size for compensatory and punitive awards). Defense costs, settlements driven by optics, loss of leadership continuity, stock-price reaction, and cultural damage frequently dominate. Individual managers are rarely personally liable under Title VII, but the company is, and the CEO almost always loses his job.

Bottom line: A truly mutual, disclosed, and carefully managed relationship can sometimes avoid catastrophe, but the combination of power imbalance and direct reporting line makes it high-risk for the firm. Most sophisticated boards treat it as a governance and risk issue that should not occur, and many CEOs have lost their positions over it even when the relationship was described as consensual. Outcomes depend heavily on jurisdiction, the company’s policies, whether it was disclosed, and subsequent conduct.

posts.text:
$INTC Foundry has its first customer to officially announce EMIB, and it's $MSFT. @Microsoft will use @Intel_Foundry EMIB advanced packaging for Azure first-party silicon. To be clear, it's EMIB, not EMIB-T. There was some confusion. And the packaging piece is separate from the Xeon piece, even though both sit under one long-term agreement.

What was announced:
- EMIB packaging for Microsoft's own custom Azure silicon (Cobalt and or Maia) 
- Multi-year Xeon supply capacity, including next-gen Diamond Rapids
- Xeon work in Azure on CXL memory, QuickAssist and TDX confidential computing
- No terms, volumes or timing

Some thoughts:
-Packaging is the door into foundry. It's a smaller commitment than wafers and it goes straight at a real bottleneck. I've been saying the transistor isn't what limits AI anymore. Power, memory and packaging are.
-Somebody had to go first. No one wants to be the first company to put its name on non TSMC, and now someone has. I'll be honest: I had Google and AWS as the likely first packaging announcements. Microsoft got there first.
-This is the follow-through I was looking for. @LipBuTan1 has said he won't spend capex without a customer commitment, and on the October call he said a couple of packaging customers would be ready to announce in the next two quarters. Less than three weeks later, here's the first one.
-The Xeon piece matters on its own. Agents need CPUs, and Intel says supply stays tight into 2028. Locking in multi-year capacity, Diamond Rapids included, is Microsoft buying supply insurance.
-What's missing: terms, volumes and which chips exactly. Packaging gets Intel in the door. Wafers, 14A above all, are where foundry makes its money, and I still think that's 2029 or 2030.

Congrats to the Intel Foundry folks.

Our office is investigating whether Huang's actions have resulted in harms to Missouri's state pension funds.

Missourians deserve to know those impacting their hard-earned retirement savings are not in bed with a Chinese spy."

The post rides on a quoted earlier post about Huang's admission and the board's independent investigation. At my read it had about 800 impressions and 3 likes, so the room caught it essentially at publication.

Why it matters: this is a new actor class in the case. Everything so far has been federal (Congress, Commerce/DOJ, the SEC probe) or private (the Kistenmacher class action). Hanaway is the first state attorney general to open a pension-harm track, which is the state-level securities and fiduciary route the Reuters liability analysis flagged on 11/11 as available but unused ("No states have brought claims"). It also fits her office's current line of work: last week she sued ISS over ESG proxy voting, framed explicitly around protecting Missouri pension returns, and the Missouri State Auditor published a report this month on the state's eight largest pension systems and their proxy voting. Whether it becomes a books-and-records demand, a Martin Act-style state investigation, or stays a press posture is the open question; the post itself announces an investigation, not a filing.
-------------------------------
NVIDIA: HOW PENSIONS AND ENDOWMENTS WOULD SUE TO BE COMPENSATED

Four routes, plus a fifth that costs the funds nothing. In practice a big pension runs them in sequence, not in parallel.

1. THE FEDERAL SECURITIES CLASS ACTION, AS LEAD PLAINTIFF

This is the main money route. The claim is Rule 10b-5, with Section 20(a) control-person claims against Huang and the directors personally: Nvidia and Huang allegedly misled the market, the Oct 9, 2025 denial of the Megaspeed reporting being the anchor statement, and the stock's fall on the corrective disclosures (down 8.8% intraday on Nov 9, roughly $192B erased) is the loss. That case already exists: Kistenmacher v. Nvidia, filed in federal court in San Jose. Under the PSLRA, the investor with the largest financial interest in the class period (Oct 9, 2025 to Nov 8, 2026 on the current complaint) is presumptively appointed lead plaintiff, and that slot is built for institutions. MOSERS or PSRS/PEERS would file a lead-plaintiff motion by the Jan 8, 2027 deadline, take control of the case from the individual filer, pick the law firm, and negotiate the fee. Endowments do the same when their direct holdings are large enough, though most ride as class members because their Nvidia sits inside manager accounts.

2. OPTING OUT AND SUING ALONE

If a fund's documented losses are big enough, it often exits the class and files its own action, 10b-5 plus state blue-sky claims (most state securities acts, Missouri's included, give a defrauded purchaser a direct damages or rescission claim). It keeps the whole recovery instead of sharing pro rata with every index holder on earth, and it controls settlement timing. Korea's National Pension Service, with an $8.9B position and a paper loss in the billions, is the profile that usually gets this pitch from the plaintiffs' bar. The tradeoff: it bears its own costs and the loss-causation fight alone.

3. DELAWARE: A SECTION 220 DEMAND, THEN A DERIVATIVE SUIT

posts.text:
Ok. This is actually insane.

Someone is willing to pay me $1,413 just for agreeing to buy $TSLA at $350 by January 15.

It's called a cash-secured put, and here's how it works.

$TSLA is trading around $385. I can sell a $350 put expiring January 15, 2027 and collect $1,413 upfront.

In return, I agree to buy 100 shares at $350 if the stock is below that price at expiration.

That means I need $35,000 in cash set aside to cover the purchase. That's where the "cash-secured" part comes from.

Here's what can happen:

1. $TSLA stays above $350.

The contract expires worthless, I keep the entire $1,413, and I never have to buy the shares. That's a 4.0% return on my $35,000 in 58 days.

2. $TSLA falls below $350.

I buy 100 shares at $350. But because I collected $1,413 upfront, my real cost is $335.87 per share. That's almost 13% below where Tesla trades today.

Of course, there's risk.

If $TSLA drops to $300, I'd be sitting on a $3,588 unrealized loss.

But someone who bought 100 shares at today's $385 price would be down about $8,500.

And Tesla's next earnings report is expected after this put expires, so there's no earnings surprise in the middle of the trade.

This is how investors get paid while waiting to buy stocks at prices they're comfortable with.

Not financial advice. Just sharing how options work.

Follow me if you found this helpful.

$ANT $MU $SNDK $LITE ANTHROPIC INDEX INCLUSION: HOW THE RULES CHANGED IN 2026

2026 is the year the index industry rewired itself for the mega-IPO wave. SpaceX was the test case in June, and Anthropic is the second deal through the new machinery. Every major provider except the S&P 500 now has a fast lane measured in trading days. The S&P 500 looked at the same changes, formally consulted on them, and refused.

THE DEAL THE INDEXES HAVE TO DIGEST

Anthropic prices tonight and trades tomorrow, Thu 11/19, on Nasdaq as ANT. 825M Class A shares at a $70 to $78 range against roughly 13.1B total shares, so a market cap of about $916B to $1.02T at the range, roughly $1.4T fully diluted, with talk of pricing above the range. The critical number for index purposes is not the trillion. It is the float: only about 6% of the shares are in the public offering. Another $26B goes in a private placement to strategic holders (Alphabet and Nvidia about $10B each, AMD $2.5B, Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft $1B each, TSMC $500M, per MarketWatch), and Alphabet ends up owning about 13%. Insiders are locked up 180 days with staggered early releases. The founders control 50.1% of the votes through a single share, and the S-1 itself warns the multi-class structure may make the stock ineligible for some indices. So the index question is: what does each provider do with a trillion-dollar company where only about $60B of stock actually trades?

THE OLD WORLD

Historically an IPO seasoned. The S&P 500 required 12 months of trading plus a profitability test. The Nasdaq-100 required three full calendar months, not counting the listing month, so a November IPO waited for the December annual reconstitution at best and usually the following year. Russell added IPOs at quarterly maintenance, typically two to five months after listing. The one exception was MSCI, which has had an early-inclusion rule for very large IPOs since 2007: meet a size test at 1.8x the segment cutoff and you can enter at the close of the tenth trading day. For two decades the system was designed to let a stock find its level, survive its lockup, and only then become forced buying for passive money.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2026, PROVIDER BY PROVIDER

NASDAQ-100 (EFFECTIVE MAY 1, 2026)

This is the biggest change. A new Fast Entry rule: if a new listing's full market cap ranks in the top 40 of current constituents when tested at the close of its seventh trading day, Nasdaq announces the addition after the tenth trading day and adds it after the fifteenth, without removing anyone, so the index can temporarily hold more than 100 names. Two supporting changes matter as much as the headline. The 10% minimum free float, itself only introduced in June 2024, was eliminated entirely. And the weighting formula was rewritten for low-float giants: weight is based on a modified market cap equal to the price times the lesser of total shares outstanding or three times the free-float shares. A 6% float therefore gets weighted as if it were 18% of the company. Nasdaq's own FAQ worked the exact hypothetical: a $1T company floating 6% enters at about a 1% weight, and tracking funds must buy roughly $6B of stock, about 10% of the entire available float. Anthropic is that hypothetical with a ticker. There is no profitability test in the Nasdaq-100, and average daily traded value only needs to clear $5M.

FTSE RUSSELL US (EFFECTIVE MAY 26, 2026)

Russell added fast entry after the fifth trading day for IPOs whose investable (float-adjusted) market cap clears the Russell Top 500 breakpoint; for Anthropic the stated threshold is $17.942B of investable cap, which a $60B float clears easily. Weight is on investable cap only, no 3x multiplier, and the IPO must have at least 5% of shares public at listing or within 12 months. Russell's reconstitution is now semi-annual, June and December, which matters for the timing below.

posts.name: Alphatica
posts.text:
Anthropic starts trading tomorrow. $81.3 billion at $83 a share. The largest IPO in history, ahead of SpaceX's $75B in June.

The market has already paid for it. SPY is −5.55% over the last 20 trading days. QQQ is −9.06%.

The question now: does the drain keep going once $81 billion is in one stock, or was the selling the drain?

We tested it. 54 of the largest US-listed IPOs since 2007. SPY and QQQ forward returns from each listing-day close.

In the 20 trading days after listing, mega-IPOs haven't drained liquidity. The market has done better than usual.

-SPY 20-day forward: +1.90%, 83% win rate (p < 0.0001)
-QQQ 20-day forward: +2.44%, 80% win rate (p = 0.0001)

SPY on any random day: +0.78% over 20 days. After a mega-IPO it beats its own baseline by +1.12% (p = 0.004).

The $15B+ tier: Visa +5.16%, GM +3.62%, Meta +3.59%, Alibaba -6.09%. Three of four positive.

Now the live tests. 2026 gave us two IPOs bigger than anything in the study:

1. SpaceX ($75B, June 12): SPY +1.36%, QQQ -0.23% over 20 days.
2. SK hynix ($26.5B, July 10): SPY +2.43%, QQQ -0.34%.

SPY rose both times, short of the +1.90% average. QQQ was flat both times. No drain. But no tech-led rally either.

Our study starts at the listing, so it can't tell us whether the selling was caused by the IPO. The closest precedent is Meta in 2012: SPY fell −4.98% in the 20 days before, then rose +3.59% in the 20 after. 

The caveat: Anthropic is 3.7x Alibaba, the largest IPO in our historical sample. Two live tests is not a sample. The direction has held. The magnitude at this scale is still an open question.

The 20-day clock starts at tomorrow's close. We'll post the result either way.

posts.name: Anthony Pompliano 🌪
posts.text:
Personal sovereignty is about to be very important.

This trend started with the launch of bitcoin, which gave individuals the ability to store and transact monetary value without the interference of governments or corporations. 

Hundreds of millions of people have flocked to the asset around the world. "Be your own bank" became a rallying cry for an entire generation that was tired of undisciplined monetary policy and greasy fingers of politicians. 

This idea of sovereignty is not going to stop there though.

You can see sovereignty of your queries and ideas being popularized by @VeniceAI. They give people the ability to tap into leading models, but they put privacy and security at the heart of their product. 

Who doesn't want to tap into the power of superhuman intelligence without the prying eyes of big tech companies?

Sovereignty won't stop there. @Apple has pioneered incredible consumer privacy and sovereignty over personal data, including biometric security features and on-device data storage. Putting consumers in charge of their data will always be a popular strategy. 

You even see people thinking about sovereignty as they get more into "prepping" in light of recent downed services and outages. They don't want to count on others to ensure they are safe, warm, fed, and hydrated. 

Lastly, we are hyper-focused on giving individuals sovereignty over their investment portfolio at @cfosilvia. Many people are tired of corporations or financial advisors telling them what to do with their money, instead they want to educate themselves and make the allocation decisions.

This doesn't mean that an individual won't work with an accountant, tax expert, or even a financial advisor, but it does mean that the individual will have control and dictate their plan to the vendors to carry out. 

As AI becomes more prevalent, I suspect that products will have to make an important decision...do you give users sovereignty or do you extract value from the user into your product?

Those who prioritize sovereignty will have a substantial advantage. 

@Shopify talks about "arming the rebels." I think that is a great framework for companies to pursue.

Give power to the people. Have technology serve them, rather than people serving corporations. 

This is where most of the value will be for the next decade.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on why the company offered buyouts to around 60,000 employees:

The buyouts were meant to give employees a sense of agency in making their own career choices.

Microsoft isn't treating software engineers as obsolete. Software engineering will "thrive," but the way teams are organized and the work engineers do will change significantly with AI.

Employees will increasingly become managers of AI agents and systems that produce the work, with this shift expected across all jobs.

One Microsoft team of just 11 developers building Cowork now builds "a software factory that builds the product," rather than building the product directly.

As a 51-year-old incumbent, Microsoft isn't an AI-first company. The transition to AI-driven workflows will take longer than many expect, and some employees may choose to leave.

Elon Musk on why the historic Starship catch is a much bigger milestone than most people realize

“Catching the ship was the final major piece”

SpaceX has now achieved:

• 3 successful Super Heavy booster catches
• A booster that was reflown and caught again
• The FIRST EVER Starship upper-stage catch
• Ship 42 returning from orbit in good enough condition to be reflown with only minor repairs

For the first time, SpaceX has demonstrated that both stages of Starship can return and be recovered by the launch tower

And Elon confirmed that Ship 42 will likely be preserved for public display because of its historic achievement

“No one has ever taken a stage like that and created a truly reusable upper stage and certainly not brought it back to land propulsively while being caught by giant chopsticks”

Now look at what full and rapid reusability is expected to unlock:

• Up to 100 TIMES lower cost of accessing space
• The potential to deliver MILLIONS OF TONS of payload to orbit annually
• A transportation system where both stages return, refuel, and fly again

That's the scale of what SpaceX is building

Starship has already demonstrated the recovery of both stages. The next step is turning recovery into routine, rapid reuse

And that's what will fundamentally change the economics of spaceflight

@robin_j_brooks  just flagged the most important decoupling in macro: the dollar is surging, but it is NOT tracking rate differentials. This is a credit event signal, not a rates trade.

The evidence stack:

• DXY hit 103.638, highest since April 2025—but 2y2y forward rate differentials are flat. The dollar is rising on something else.
• SOFR has been above IORB since Oct 23, with SOFR−IORB, SOFR−ON RRP, and SOFR−EFFR all above the 90th percentile since 2021. Money funds have drained ON RRP. Repo is now leaning on bank reserves.
• CCC spreads have blown out ~330bps to over 1,400bps. This is credit-quality stress, not duration stress.
• EUR 3m cross-currency basis is -2.1bp—no offshore funding panic yet. But the onshore plumbing is tightening.
• Gold -3%, silver -7%, copper -11% this month. Hard assets are being sold for cash—the classic liquidity signature.
• Indonesia rupiah at record low 18,204/USD, but EM FX broadly stable. Stress is concentrated, not systemic.

I have to agree with take here: this has the whiff of a credit event somewhere. The dollar is the smoke alarm, not the fire.

Which breaks first: the repo market, CCC credit, or the Fed's credibility?

Elon Musk reveals Grok 4.8 is in the RL phase, and that what users get from Grok Bot is at times different versions of Grok being tested for usefulness

“So this is kind of a long answer, but we are working on Grok 4.8 right now. It’s in the RL phase. And we do sort of periodic soft releases under Grok Bot.”

“So what you’ll experience with Grok Bot at times is actually various versions of Grok under the hood that we’re testing to determine its usefulness. Is it solving the user’s problem? And then using that data, whether it did or did not solve the problem, to improve Grok.”

quoted.text:
Elon Musk says xAI might now have “the best training stack software in the world” after rewriting everything from scratch over six to eight months

“And this meant rewriting the entire training, RL and inference stack from scratch, versus using JAX and SGLang, which is sort of kind of freeware from Google, more or less, but not as good as what they’ve got internally by far. So you just can’t build world class AI using mediocre freeware, to state the obvious.”

“So we’ve been rewriting the entire training stack. When I say the entire training stack, I mean everything. We’re using primarily C and some C++, because we wanna get as close to the bare metal as possible in order to extract the highest performance from the hardware. The more layers of software abstraction that you have, the less performant your code will be. And it also tends to be more of a black box, where you’re not quite sure what’s going on with the third-party software.”

posts.text: Another thing I've learned on the same topic recently, while listening to a Bernstein analyst on @OddLotsShow (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DF2i8Z4na4Y), is that many semiconductor companies made this change in how they reporting revenue and not just Nvidia.

quoted.text:
It is hard to do justice to just how bizarre this story is.  

Last year, the FT cried foul because Nvidia's disclosures attributed 22% of sales to Singapore. The FT and others questioned this figure as suspiciously implausible, given the size of Singapore's market. The explanation was simple. Multinational buyers used Singapore affiliates to centralize invoicing, while physical shipments went elsewhere. Nvidia explicitly disclosed this context in its FY2025 annual report. 

In Q3, Nvidia switched to reporting revenue by customer headquarters, rather than billing address. This resulted in Singapore ceasing to be a material line item. Nvidia explained that, because billing addresses “often reflected a customer’s centralized invoicing location, even though our products were almost always shipped elsewhere,” reporting by customer headquarters “provides a better representation of the geographic profile of our revenue.” Nvidia also recast prior periods on the same basis. 

Now, the Financial Times runs the false headline: “Nvidia stopped disclosing Singapore sales as revenues hit $104bn.” The sales still are disclosed but based on where customers are headquartered rather than location of accounts-payable departments. The same FT that faulted Nvidia for doing the latter rather than former, is now faulting Nvidia for doing the former rather than the latter. 

What is even weirder is that Nvidia continued to disclose the prior Singapore-booked metric in the  financial statements file

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Saying people use reserves is like saying that London Gold Vault depositors use the gold when they actually use paper gold certificates. Everyday market participants buy, sell, and settle trades entirely in gold certificates. They never touch or transport 27-pound gold bars. Only the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) clearing banks move or reassign the physical bullion in the central vault to balance the net claims between trading desks at the end of the day. 

If you trade a gold certificate you never "used" the gold. You used the certificate. Only the LBMA uses them just as banks use reserves. It's the same exact thing with central bank reserves.

quoted.text:
Starlink is taking home internet customers from America's biggest providers, and the numbers are getting difficult to ignore.

ST3 Insights estimates 120,114 Americans switched to Starlink in Q3, while roughly 29,000 left. That's a net gain of roughly 91,000, or four customers gained for every one lost. And that's only across the eight largest providers. ST3's founder puts total incoming customers above 150,000.

– Where are they coming from?

The biggest losses are from 5G home internet. T-Mobile, Verizon, and AT&T lost roughly 41,000 customers to Starlink, while gaining just 6,500 back, a ratio of more than 6 to 1.

The pattern extends to cable. Starlink took roughly 45,000 customers from Spectrum and Comcast's Xfinity, against 16,700 going the other way.

In other words, the same carriers fighting SpaceX over phone spectrum to contain Starlink are already losing home internet customers to it.

– Why is fixed wireless struggling?

The problem is that it runs on whatever capacity the phone network has left over. As a result, T-Mobile warns that congestion can significantly reduce speeds, while Verizon's CEO says it won't sell the service where it can't deliver adequate performance.

By contrast, Starlink's advantage isn't peak speed, but increasingly consistent performance as SpaceX resolves equipment shortages and adds capacity.

– What do the carriers say?

Charter reports no meaningful share loss to Starlink; Verizon says it sees "no discernible impact."

Further evidence that this is 2008, not 1999

Seeing AR balances rise this much, this fast is unprecedented. That reflects hundreds of of billions of revenue that has not been paid, largely to customers that have been propped up by generous financing terms and ample credit/venture markets. This becomes the proxy for leverage from the base of the pyramid and now even the most profitable players in the value chain (semis) need to start tightening their payment terms or risk running out of cash.

Now that capital spigot is shutting down - across nvidia, credit markets and eventually in VC. As that happens, you see massive mark downs on debt/AR (already happening) and every player in the value chain goes into capital preservation mode. Capital throughput draws to a halt and growth doesn’t just slow…top line falls off a cliff. This is why semis are so cyclical, because their earnings look particularly strong in periods where demand outstrips supply, but they tend to overdevelop / overextend at the tail end of those cycles, and utilization / pricing / profitably fall dramatically when customers can no longer afford more chips and you can no longer afford to extend them more credit.

posts.text:
SK HYNIX: THE 350,000-SHARE-A-DAY BID

A claim circulating today says SK hynix repurchased exactly 350,000 of its own shares on both November 16 and 17, with net buying by other corporations of 353,990, 340,056 and 347,796 shares across November 16 to 18. The numbers hold up, with one framing correction.

THE BUYBACK IS REAL, AND IT IS THE SECOND ONE

The 40 trillion won program approved on August 19 is not the buyer here. It finished a month early, in October, with 23,693,272 shares repurchased for cancellation. The current bid is the follow-on program: 20 trillion won approved on October 28 alongside third-quarter results, buying since October 29 at roughly 354 billion won a session. At about 1,000,000 won a share, that is about 350,000 shares a day, and the identical print on consecutive days is the signature of a mechanical program execution, not discretionary buying.

ONE BID, NOT TWO

KRX books an issuer's own on-market treasury purchases inside the "other corporations" investor category. The corporate net-buying line is therefore, in substance, the buyback itself seen through the flow table, plus a small residual from other corporates. Read as two series, the same demand gets counted twice.

SIZE AND RUNWAY

Roughly $240M a day, high single digits of SK hynix's daily volume: a price-insensitive bid that appears every session regardless of the tape. At 354 billion won a session, the 20 trillion won program runs about 56 sessions from October 29, which exhausts it around mid-to-late January 2027.

Korea has rehearsed the ending once already. When the first program completed early in October, local coverage immediately flagged the supply-demand gap it would leave behind. A buyback of this size is a floor with an expiry date, not a permanent feature of the float, and the trade changes the day the program does.

posts.text:
JPMORGAN IS TRYING TO SELL $2B OF QUALTRICS DEBT AT A 20% DISCOUNT

JPMorgan is marketing bonds tied to Qualtrics' $6.75B acquisition of Press Ganey Forsta at around 80 cents on the dollar, per FT.

The proposed terms:
• Maturity: 6.5 years
• Coupon: 8%
• Issue price: 80 cents on the dollar
• Implied yield: 12% to 13%

A group of banks, including JPMorgan, has been stuck holding more than $5B of acquisition debt since March after investors pulled back from software financing amid fears that AI could disrupt these businesses.

The banks had committed to providing the financing but couldn't sell the debt to outside investors, forcing them to fund the acquisition themselves.

JPMorgan is now trying to offload part of that debt before year-end, with the new bond sale expected to launch after Thanksgiving. Pricing is not yet final.

Qualtrics' existing term loan maturing in 2030 was also trading at around 82 cents on the dollar on Tuesday.

For comparison, cybersecurity firm Proofpoint just sold $2B of debt, including $1.25B in high-yield bonds that attracted more than $7B in orders and priced at an approximately 8.75% yield.

posts.text:
Micron presentation notes:

Micron says its 26 SCAs won't get broken like past LTAs. They expect stacked 3D DRAM in 2028-2029, and shareholder returns start Dec 9th.

Memory and AI:

Buyers now judge AI hardware by memory or bandwidth per dollar, not just compute. 
Compute has outpaced memory bandwidth for 20 years, so processors sit idle waiting on data. 
Customer conversations have moved from price and volume to performance, capacity and bandwidth. 
A TSMC ASIC qualified elsewhere often has to be modified to work thinned, with TSVs, inside an HBM stack. That creates a new barrier to entry.

SCAs:

26 signed, mostly 5-year, take-or-pay, with cash deposits and some fixed pricing bands. 
$32B in upfront cash and financial commitments. 
Customer demand exceeded what Micron could commit. Supply isn't expected to catch up soon. 
Sanjay doesn't expect customers to try to exit in a 2028-2029 downturn, given CEO-level negotiation, memory's ROI and joint roadmaps.

Stacked DRAM:

Memory stacked on a logic base die means high switching costs and a non-commodity product. 
Startups working on it: D-Matrix, Fractal and one in stealth. 
Thermals are the main challenge, since DRAM sits on a hot GPU. 
Starts in 2028-2029, with broad adoption by 2030-2031. Edge devices are also a target.

Nvidia:

Co-developed HBM3E and HBM4. The partnership is expected to continue through Nvidia's leadership transition.

Capital returns:

CHIPS Act restrictions expire Dec 9th. Excess cash goes to shareholders after R&D and manufacturing. 
Micron cites over $250B of US investment as the only US memory maker.
 One speaker floated keeping $200-$250B on the balance sheet and possibly taking Micron private in a downturn.

posts.text:
Sharing some strategy:

I believe that 100% of short term moves in the market are emotionally driving mostly by big funds trading macro or headlines. I also believe that 100% of long term moves in any company are fundamentally driven. That makes me naturally contrarian. If everyone loves something, I will probably dislike it. If everyone hates something, I will probably be interested. 

The key is something I learned reading about legends like Howard Marks and John Templeton. They said a great investors must be Contrarian and also be Right. Right being the key. This is why I use my strategy to buy the most beaten down themes in the market which still have the strongest growth fundamentals. 

I think Fintech is a good example of this. Its down about 40% from its peaks as a sector over the past year. Yet, every company I follow posted greater than 30% revenue growth. The stocks get cheaper as the businesses get stronger. Biotech was like that in its bear market of 2022 to 2025. Select parts of tech are getting like that. SaaS had a huge bear market in late 2025 to 2026.

Now it happens to be the data center space which I find this a bit oxymoronic though. The companies spending the most money and taking on record levels of debt are trading at record premiums while the companies selling them hundreds of billions in parts are hitting 52 week lows. That is the contrarian type of bet I am looking for.

posts.text:
I believe the @nvidia board is not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties. 

What we know is that the board fired Jensen or forced his resignation for violating company policy and/or in response to the accusation of an affair with a spy. 

They did so without careful consideration of the impact on the company, its customers, its shareholders or other stakeholders. 

They rushed to judgment without the benefit of careful due diligence or even with a basic understanding of the facts. 

How do we know this? 

We know this by how quickly Jensen was fired and how little was known at the time of his firing. 

It takes time to convene a board meeting.  There was time, maybe, for one Zoom. 

And this is a decision that should have been made by a board sitting in person and carefully deliberating the facts once they are known.  

And they should have slept on the decision and met again the day after to discuss the facts, the risks and the other implications of their decision. 

The timing and lack of information did not allow for careful board deliberation. 

While boards can fire a CEO for an inappropriate relationship with a subordinate, it should not be an automatic decision. That is why we have boards comprised of humans and not agents. 

A board should consider whether or not such a relationship was consensual or whether it was an abuse of power dynamics. And a board has to consider what the impact of the firing is on all stakeholders. 

If I were in this board, I would not have rushed to judgment based on articles in the media. I would have made sure the board had all of the facts so it could make a careful and informed decision. 

Boards of Delaware companies have a duty of care which means they must make informed, prudent and good faith decisions. This clearly did not happen here. 

What law firm is advising this board?  

Or is the board even taken good legal advice? 

It doesn’t look like it. 

And now the board is compounding its failures by insisting that there is no possibility for Jensen’s return as CEO. 

Why is it in the best interest of the company to foreclose the possibility of Jensen’s return and to do so before all of the facts are known? This is yet another breach of their duty of care. 

Furthermore, the board has launched an investigation whose scope is unknown. Investigations can be extremely damaging to a company and should be carefully targeted to address whatever facts need to be known rather than be overly broad in scope. 

In short, this looks like a series of major governance failures by directors that panicked due to headlines in the media. They likely felt compelled to do something because they were afraid of looking bad in the media, not because it was the right thing for them company. 

They couldn’t stand the heat. 

The board’s conduct here is shocking for a company of this scale and importance to our country and the world at large, particularly at this moment in history.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
This is basic accounting. When you have a bank deposit you hold an asset and the bank has a liability. Reserves are an asset for the bank and a liability of the Fed. But the Fed's liability is to the bank, not to you. You don't have a claim on reserves because they aren't your asset and they aren't the bank's liability to you. Your claim is on the bank, full stop.

You can't even hold reserves. Only banks and a handful of other institutions with Fed accounts can. When you send money to someone at another bank, your bank settles with their bank in reserves. Your deposit goes away and they get a new one, but the reserves never touch your hands.

The one time you end up holding a Fed liability is when you withdraw cash. Your bank swaps reserves for paper currency and hands it to you. That's a Fed liability, but it's a different one. It isn't reserves.

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
The dollar’s continued strength despite the technology selloff is particularly revealing. Deutsche Bank data show aggressive overseas buying of U.S. equity ETFs during the decline. These foreign investors include international pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurance companies, and other institutions based outside the United States.

Much of this buying reflects America’s dominance in global equity benchmarks, expectations that U.S. corporations will continue capturing a disproportionate share of global profits, and institutional portfolio rebalancing during market corrections. Dollar appreciation can also benefit unhedged foreign investors, while elevated American interest rates and global rate differentials continue supporting the currency.

But these inflows may be temporarily cushioning U.S. equities even as underlying financial conditions deteriorate. Importantly, foreign ETF inflows do not necessarily represent entirely new dollar demand, since investors may already hold dollars or hedge their currency exposure. The broader concern is how dependent American financial markets have become on sustained international capital flows, particularly with valuations heavily concentrated in technology and AI.

If foreign investors begin withdrawing capital while the Fed continues tightening, equities could lose an important source of support precisely when dollar financing becomes more expensive for overseas borrowers. That could accelerate global deleveraging and intensify selling across financial markets. Dollar strength alone doesn’t establish a liquidity crisis, but if foreign inflows reverse while the dollar continues appreciating and offshore funding costs rise, it would become a much more serious warning of an emerging global dollar squeeze.

quoted.text: "Why is the dollar rallying even as US tech stocks have sold off so much?" asks Deutsche Bank's George Saravelos, who expected the opposite would happen. His explanation: rate differentials and the fact that foreigners have been big buyers of the US equity dip, at least for now

Copper's sell-off today is a timely moment that reinforces a point I made on @business last week. 

As I told @VonnieQuinn, I've been pounding the table on copper for years, but right now I'm cautious.

Why? Because of dollar liquidity.

We're seeing a dollar shortage developing across global markets, which is being driven by a mix of pressures from AI-related debt issuance, volatility in the equity market and the extraordinary costs associated with energy security - a topic I've discussed in some detail this year.

All of those combine to ensure that copper is particularly exposed. A stronger dollar constrains China's ability to ease monetary conditions, putting further pressure on credit and economic growth. At the same time, companies needing to raise dollars are forced to liquidate commodity inventories, which piles on further pressure on prices.

Commodities are driven by two fears - scarcity and debasement. One is the fear of running out of the commodity, the other is fear of running out of money. In a time where liquidity becomes the major concern, even hard assets like copper get sold in order to raise cash.

It's important to keep hold of the fact however that the long-term drivers of the commodity supercyle have not disappeared: the case for investing in copper comes in the continued need for electrification and deglobalisation - demand for neither will suddenly go away.

posts.name: Art Berman
posts.text:
OPEC Demand and EIA Production Growth Suggest a Temporary Oil Surplus in 2Q 2027

I tested several methods of extending OPEC's supply data through 2027 using OPEC's own production projections and EIA growth assumptions. 

I selected the relatively high EIA supply trajectory to remain consistent with mainstream expectations of production recovery.

The different methods converge near 110 mmb/d by late 2027. Even under these assumptions, the projected surplus is concentrated in 2Q 2027, with the market returning to approximate balance in the second half.

A temporary surplus is not evidence of a sustained oil glut.

Substantial deficits preceded the projected surplus. That makes the cumulative inventory balance at least as important as the quarterly flow balance.

The conclusion isn't that the mainstream outlook is wrong about production recovery. It's that production recovery, a temporary surplus and an oil glut are three different things.

You're not describing reality accurately. What you’re describing is a model where the Fed and Treasury are consolidated. That can be a useful simplification, but it isn’t how the system actually operates. The Fed can’t lend to the Treasury directly or let the TGA run an overdraft. The law requires it to buy Treasuries in the open market.

In practice, the Treasury has to have funds in the TGA before it spends. Tax receipts and bond sales are what put them there. You might say this doesn't matter, but no court in the USA cares about MMT's opinions on this. The law is the law and the laws dictate the bounds of operational reality. 

I called the explanation sloppy because of those operational details, not as a personal shot. Maybe I should just call them "problematic" as Wray did in his paper....

Global refined product markets face a prolonged supply shortfall, and Russia is the swing factor in how long it lasts.

According to Kpler, damage and export constraints in the Mideast Gulf and a shift towards petrochemical yields in China have cut supply East of Suez. Atlantic Basin refiners are running flat out in response, with US #diesel and jet fuel exports to Europe up nearly 60% year on year since March, but they have offset only about a quarter of the loss.
